Supreme Court declines to restore policy allowing immigration judges to close deportation cases
(ABC NEWS) — The Supreme Court declined to unfreeze a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration judges to use their discretion to temporarily close deportation cases for immigrants.
In an unsigned order, the court rejected a request from three cities with large migrant populations — Baltimore as well as Columbus, Ohio and New Haven, Connecticut — to pause an agreement between Texas and the Trump administration that threw out the policy.
The regulation, known as “administrative closure,” gives immigration judges discretion to temporarily pause deportation proceedings for migrants while the migrants seek humanitarian protections or other forms of legal status in the country.
The Trump administration has pushed to curtail judicial processes for unlawful migrants, and the high court’s conservative majority has been largely deferential to executive authority in the area of immigration policy.
Deportation hearings in immigration court are legal proceedings initiated by the Department of Homeland Security in which an immigration judge determines whether a migrant should be removed from the United States. Often, an immigration judge will pause or dismiss a case to allow the individual to pursue legal relief.
While dismissals were viewed as a positive outcome for migrants, immigration attorneys have said the Trump administration, as part of its immigration crackdown, began to use dismissals to detain people at immigration courts and place them into expedited removal without allowing them to fight their case.
Last year, federal agents arrested hundreds of migrants at immigration courts — in some cases after their deportation cases were dismissed.
In court filings, the cities argued that administrative closure promoted “efficiency” and protected “due process rights.” They also argued that the practice has existed in various forms for decades.

U.S. Supreme Court leaves in place limits on when deportation cases can be paused

by Uriel J. García, The Texas Tribune
October 27, 2026

Immigration judges are still barred from pausing deportation proceedings — even if an immigrant qualifies for legal status — after the U.S. Supreme Court declined Tuesday to intervene in a Texas-led lawsuit that challenged the delays.

At issue is a federal rule the Biden administration revived in 2024 that allowed immigration judges to postpone deportation proceedings for immigrants who qualify for legal status in the U.S., either through being married to a U.S. citizen or certain visas for victims of crime.

On June 22, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit in the Northern District of Texas in Wichita Falls to block the Biden administration’s immigration rule, arguing in a 43-page lawsuit that it effectively granted “indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country.”

Lawsuits usually take several months to years to settle. But in this case, U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor ruled the same day in favor of Texas after the Department of Justice, under the Trump administration, filed its response saying it agreed with Paxton’s office.

Three cities — Baltimore; New Haven, Conn.; and Columbus, Ohio — and Centro Legal de la Raza, an Oakland, Calif.,-based nonprofit that provides legal services, filed a lawsuit challenging the judge’s decision. They argued the rule was approved by Congress, giving authority to immigration judges to halt deportation proceedings for immigrants who have pending applications and qualify for legal status.

The plaintiffs said that crime victims who are undocumented might stop cooperating with local law enforcement if they are at risk of being deported, even if they qualify for specific visas that help them stay in the country during the criminal prosecution. The cities also argued that they could lose tax revenue if their residents are deported.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court issued a one-sentence ruling denying a request from the plaintiffs to protect the procedures that had been in place during the Biden administration.

The case can go back to a lower court to decide if the cities can intervene, or the cities can ask the Supreme Court to have a hearing.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

sources.news_title: SCOTUS Rejects Bid To Revive Lax Biden-Era Deportation Rule
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to restore a Biden-era regulation allowing for certain deportation proceedings to be temporarily paused. The decision was seemingly unanimous.
In its unsigned order, the high court rejected an emergency application by three Democrat-led cities to pause a consent judgment between the Justice Department and Texas. As described by SCOTUSblog, the agreement ended a Biden-era regulation that permitted “immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings — when, for example, a crime victim or witness is seeking immigration relief, such as asylum — while the challengers’ appeal in the lower federal courts is ongoing.”
Texas initially sued to end the rule in a lawsuit against the DOJ, which agreed with the Lone Star State and subsequently requested a federal judge to invalidate it. The agreement to end the regulation was approved by Texas-based Chief District Judge Reed O’Connor, a Bush 43 appointee.
Three cities — Baltimore, Maryland; Columbus, Ohio; and New Haven, Connecticut — joined the legal battle along with Centro Legal de la Raza, a leftist-funded immigration group, in an attempt to uphold the Biden-era rule. O’Connor rejected their request to do so on the grounds that they lack standing. He more specifically dismissed the cities’ argument that “the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported,” according to SCOTUSblog.
The 5th Circuit Court of Appeals also rejected the challengers’ emergency request to pause the DOJ and Texas’ consent judgment.
In the administration’s brief before SCOTUS, U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer accused the cities of attempting “to improperly leverage a clear-cut dispute over intervention into a far-reaching attack on the merits of a consent judgment.” He further echoed arguments that the challengers lack standing to bring their request.
“For that same reason — and because they have failed to establish any irreparable harm pending the appeal of the denial of their motion to intervene — a stay pending appeal is plainly unwarranted,” the brief reads. “Objections about the merits of a consent judgment are no substitute for the threshold prerequisites of Article III standing.”
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton similarly contended in his state’s filing that the plaintiffs “fail each element of the demanding stay standard.” He also reasoned that the challengers “cannot demonstrate a reasonable probability” that the high court would agree to take up and hear the case on the merits.
The Supreme Court did not provide reasoning for its rejection of the cities’ application. There were no noted dissents in Tuesday’s order.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Allows Trump Administration to Maintain Restrictions on Immigration Judges’ Authority to Pause Deportation Cases
sources.text:
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected an emergency request to reinstate immigration judges’ authority to administratively close deportation proceedings, allowing a nationwide restriction negotiated by President Donald Trump’s administration and Texas to remain in effect while litigation continues.
The justices issued a brief, unsigned order Oct. 27 denying the request from Baltimore, Maryland; Columbus, Ohio; New Haven, Connecticut; and Centro Legal de la Raza, an immigrant legal services organization. The court provided no explanation, and no justice publicly dissented.
The decision leaves intact a June federal court judgment eliminating a 2024 Biden administration regulation that authorized immigration judges to temporarily remove certain cases from active court dockets through a procedure known as administrative closure.
Administrative closure allows an immigration judge to pause removal proceedings without dismissing the underlying case. It has historically been used when an individual is pursuing a separate immigration benefit or awaiting resolution of another legal matter that could affect the outcome of deportation proceedings.
The practice can also help courts manage large caseloads by temporarily suspending proceedings that cannot be resolved immediately.
Texas challenged the regulation June 22, arguing that it exceeded the authority granted to immigration judges under federal law.
In its lawsuit, the state maintained that administrative closure could allow individuals without lawful immigration status to remain in the United States for extended periods without a final resolution of their cases.
Texas argued that the policy effectively permitted judges to grant indefinite relief from deportation without congressional authorization.
The Trump administration agreed with the state’s interpretation rather than defending the 2024 regulation.
Federal officials and Texas subsequently submitted a joint proposal asking U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to declare the rule unlawful.
O’Connor approved the agreement the same day the lawsuit was filed, issuing a judgment that blocked enforcement of the regulation nationwide. The judgment also restricted future regulations permitting administrative closure without an express statutory basis.
The unusual speed of the proceedings became a central issue in the subsequent legal challenge.
The three cities and Centro Legal de la Raza sought permission to intervene in the case, arguing that eliminating administrative closure would harm immigrant residents and disrupt local services.
They maintained that the procedure had helped crime victims, neglected children and other immigrants whose eligibility for legal relief depended on separate applications or proceedings.
The organizations also argued that the federal government had circumvented the Administrative Procedure Act, which generally establishes public notice and comment requirements for adopting or repealing federal regulations.
In their Supreme Court filing, the challengers accused the administration of using litigation with a politically aligned state to eliminate a regulation without following ordinary administrative procedures.
“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” they wrote.
The cities described the agreement as an effort to accomplish through the courts what would otherwise require a formal regulatory process.
O’Connor rejected their attempt to intervene, concluding that they had not established the legal standing necessary to participate in the original lawsuit.
The New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals subsequently declined to suspend the judgment while the challengers pursued an appeal.
The coalition then asked the Supreme Court to intervene on an emergency basis, arguing that continued enforcement of the restriction would cause immediate harm to affected immigrants and the communities where they reside.
The Justice Department opposed the request, maintaining that the cities and advocacy organization had not established a sufficient legal interest in the dispute.
U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that the challengers were improperly attempting to use a dispute over their participation in the case to reopen the underlying judgment.
The administration and Texas also maintained that immigration judges lack statutory authority to suspend removal proceedings indefinitely.
The Supreme Court’s refusal to intervene leaves those restrictions in place but does not constitute a final ruling on the underlying legal dispute.
Administrative closure has been used in immigration courts for decades, although its availability has shifted under successive presidential administrations.
During Trump’s first term, federal officials attempted to limit immigration judges’ discretion to administratively close cases.
The Biden administration restored and formalized that authority through a regulation adopted in May 2024.
After Trump returned to office in January 2025, the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review announced that it would no longer defend the Biden administration’s regulation against a legal challenge.
The resulting agreement with Texas eliminated that regulation before the courts conducted a full adversarial examination of its legality.
According to federal statistics cited in The Washington Post’s coverage of Tuesday’s decision, approximately 360,000 immigration cases have been administratively closed since 1990.
Those cases were removed from active court schedules but not permanently dismissed, meaning they could potentially be reopened.
The June judgment has already affected immigration court proceedings nationwide.
An advisory published by the Immigrant Legal Resource Center in September reported that some immigration courts were interpreting the judgment broadly, denying requests for administrative closure and returning previously closed cases to active dockets.
The restrictions do not automatically require deportation in every affected case. Individuals may still pursue applicable forms of immigration relief, and separate procedures for postponing or resolving proceedings may remain available when authorized by law.
However, the elimination of administrative closure removes a frequently used case-management option from immigration judges.
Tuesday’s order represents another legal development in the Trump administration’s efforts to accelerate immigration enforcement and restrict discretionary mechanisms that can delay removal proceedings.
The administration maintains that immigration courts must operate within the authority established by Congress, while the cities and immigrant advocates argue that the restriction interferes with fair case management and access to lawful immigration relief.
The underlying appeal remains pending before the 5th Circuit.
Until another court changes the existing judgment, immigration judges remain barred from using the administrative-closure authority established under the Biden administration’s 2024 regulation.

sources.news_title: Court declines to restore Biden-era regulation allowing some deportation proceedings to be suspended
sources.text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to restore a Biden-era regulation that allows immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings. In a brief, unsigned order, the court turned down a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the U.S. Department of Justice that threw out the rule.
There were no noted dissents.
The regulation at the center of the dispute, which provides what is known as “administrative closure,” was adopted by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, part of the Department of Justice, in 2024. Under it, immigration judges may suspend some deportation proceedings – for example, to allow a crime victim or witness to seek relief, such as asylum, from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which is a separate agency.
In June of this year, Texas went to federal court in Wichita Falls, where its case was assigned to Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor – the only federal judge in that area. Calling the administrative-closure rule “one part of the Biden-Harris Administration’s campaign to undermine our immigration laws,” it alleged that the EOIR does not have the authority to adopt the administrative-closure rule. Instead, it wrote, federal law requires an immigration judge, at the end of a proceeding, to “decide whether an alien is removable from the United States.”
Just a few hours after the case was filed, the DOJ and Texas asked O’Connor to enter a final judgment for the state. The DOJ also asked him both to throw out the rule altogether and to issue an order making clear that the EOIR could not adopt a similar rule in the future. O’Connor granted those requests on the same day.
On Aug. 7, three cities with large immigrant populations – Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio – and Centro Legal de la Raza, which provides legal services to immigrants, filed an emergency motion to join the case so that they could defend the administrative-closure rule on appeal, when neither Texas nor the federal government intended to do so. O’Connor denied their request on the ground that they lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing. In particular, he rejected the cities’ contention that the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported.
The challengers then went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, which rejected their request to block the consent judgment between Texas and the Department of Justice and thereby reinstate the administrative-closure rule while their appeal continued.
On Oct. 9, the challengers came to the Supreme Court, calling the consent agreement the product of “egregious collusion” and asking the justices to step in. Their attorney, Joshua Salzman of Democracy Forward, argued that permitting the consent agreement to stand could have widespread implications. “If a judgment procured through such open collusion is allowed to remain in effect,” he wrote, “any agency can avoid the strictures of the” federal law governing administrative agencies “by advertising its unwillingness to defend a disfavored regulation and by immediately acquiescing to nationwide relief.”
Urging the Supreme Court to leave the agreement in place, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer contended that the challengers’ request to pause O’Connor’s ruling “attempts to improperly leverage a clear-cut dispute over” the challengers’ efforts to join the case “into a far-reaching attack on the merits of” the court’s approval of the agreement. For its part, Texas told the justices that putting O’Connor’s ruling on hold “would revive a rule the district court declared unlawful, renew the fiscal and sovereign injuries Texas alleged, and unsettle a final judgment accepted by the actual parties.”
Four days after the case was fully briefed, the court denied the challengers’ request without comment.

But there's a bit more to this story than the Supreme Court's decidedly brief order.
The dispute centers on a practice known as "administrative closure," which allows immigration judges to temporarily remove a deportation case from their active docket without actually dismissing it or deciding whether the individual should be removed from the country.
Essentially, it's a pause button. The case remains unresolved and can be returned to the active docket later.
Immigration judges have used versions of this procedure for decades, and the Biden administration issued a regulation in 2024 formally authorizing its use in certain circumstances. Supporters maintained that it allowed judges to manage their caseloads more efficiently and gave immigrants time to pursue other avenues of legal relief.
Critics, however, argued that the practice could leave deportation cases in litigation limbo indefinitely, effectively allowing individuals who might otherwise be removed to remain in the country.
Enter Texas.
On June 22, 2026, the state sued the Department of Justice (DOJ), challenging the legality of the Biden-era regulation. In a somewhat unusual turn of events, the Trump administration agreed with Texas that the rule was unlawful. And so, that very same day, U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor approved a consent judgment between the parties, vacating the regulation nationwide and barring the DOJ from enforcing it.
Which might have been the end of the matter, except that not everyone was thrilled with the arrangement. Three cities — Baltimore, Maryland; Columbus, Ohio; and New Haven, Connecticut — along with immigrant legal-services organization Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the lawsuit to defend the regulation.
They argued that the arrangement between Texas and the Trump administration effectively eliminated an existing federal rule without the usual opportunity for public participation or a meaningful judicial examination of its legality.
O'Connor denied their request to intervene, finding they hadn't demonstrated the necessary legal standing to join the case. The groups appealed to the 5th Circuit and asked the Supreme Court to temporarily block the Texas judgment while their appeal proceeds, contending that the consent agreement was the product of "egregious collusion."
As you might expect, Texas and the DOJ opposed that request, maintaining that the groups had not established a legally sufficient basis to challenge the judgment.
On Tuesday, the Supreme Court denied the emergency application, leaving the lower court's judgment undisturbed.
Now, we should note what the justices didn't do here: They didn't issue a ruling declaring administrative closure unconstitutional or definitively resolve whether immigration judges have statutory authority to use the practice. They simply declined to suspend the existing judgment while the challengers pursue their appeal.
The practical impact, however, is significant. The 2024 regulation remains off the books, and immigration judges cannot rely on it to administratively close removal proceedings. That doesn't mean every previously paused case automatically results in deportation, nor does it eliminate every other procedural mechanism for delaying or resolving a case.
But for now, the Trump administration's position prevails; the Biden-era regulation remains vacated, while the fight over who can challenge that outcome continues in the lower courts.

Allison H. Eid (concurrence)
Gregory A. Phillips (dissent)
In Vizguerra’s case, she received a deportation order in 2011, which also gave her the option of departing voluntarily. For family reasons, Vizguerra left for Mexico while her appeal was pending, which triggered a withdrawal of the appeal. After she returned to the United States in 2013 without authorization, the government reinstated the prior removal order.
Since then, the government has extended her ability to remain in the country, but immigration personnel detained her again in March 2025. Vizguerra is afraid of returning to Mexico, believing she will be persecuted or tortured based on her criticism of the Mexican government.
She also pursued withholding-only proceedings, which would prevent the government from returning her to Mexico. For years, the 10th Circuit’s precedent required people to bring petitions challenging their final removal orders after withholding-only proceedings had wrapped up.
Then, last year, the U.S. Supreme Court decided Riley v. Bondi. While the case did not involve a reinstatement order, the majority decision rejected the 10th Circuit’s practice and noted that judicially reviewable, final orders of removal have certain characteristics. In Vizguerra’s case, the government argued that Riley left the court without any ability to review reinstatement orders.
All judges on the 10th Circuit panel disagreed with that argument. Judge Carolyn B. McHugh, writing for the majority, wrote that the 10th Circuit’s precedent aligned at the time with its peer circuits in finding judges could address reinstatement orders the same as with final orders of removal. Further, the Supreme Court’s recent decision “did not clearly overrule this approach.”
“A reinstatement order has the ‘same characteristics’ emphasized in Riley, and qualifies as an order of removal,” she wrote.
However, McHugh continued for herself and Eid, the panel could not address the substance of Vizguerra’s challenge to her reinstatement order. While the 10th Circuit’s old approach required her to wait until her withholding-only proceedings were done, and the current approach suddenly rendered her challenge 12 years late, McHugh wrote that the seeming Catch-22 was avoidable.
“Ms. Vizguerra’s putative reinstatement order was issued on July 24, 2013 — well before our 2015 decision … held as a matter of first impression that orders of removal were not final until completion of withholding-only proceedings,” explained McHugh, a Barack Obama appointee. “Thus, Ms. Vizguerra’s failure to timely file her petition was not in reliance on binding case law. Nor did our case law then bar her petition for review as premature.”
Judge Gregory A. Phillips, also an Obama appointee, wrote that he would have overturned Vizguerra’s reinstatement order. He noted the language of the order made it appear that it was not, itself, a deportation order, nor did a valid underlying order exist. He also believed the 10th Circuit and the government caused the confusion over the review deadline.
“Well before Ms. Vizguerra received her administrative removal order, the government told us that such an order was unripe until the (Board of Immigration Appeals) concluded withholding-only proceedings,” Phillips wrote. “To put it metaphorically — for years, the government told us, other courts, and litigants like Ms. Vizguerra: ‘you can’t appeal until the sun goes down.’ Now it’s arguing, ‘Ms. Vizguerra needed to appeal before the sun came up.’ I wouldn’t let it.”
In her concurrence, Eid agreed that the Riley decision was “not sufficient to overrule our precedent” and deprive the 10th Circuit of the ability to review reinstatement orders categorically. But she laid out a case for a full-court hearing in which the 10th Circuit could overrule itself and shut down that path for review.
In contrast with a reviewable removal order, a reinstatement order “makes no new findings other than confirming that this is the person to whom the previous removal order applies,” she wrote. “Reinstatement orders require neither judgment nor reasoning. The outcome is predetermined based on whether the three criteria are met. Any meaningful conclusion was made during the initial removal process.”
Eid acknowledged that no other circuit court has adopted her reasoning. But she cited individual judges who have advocated for that view in recent years.
Lawyers for Vizguerra did not immediately respond to questions from Colorado Politics about the impact Eid’s position would have on immigration cases if it became law in the six-state region covered by the 10th Circuit.
However, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s statistics for fiscal year 2023 showed that it completed more than 183,000 deportations. Of those, 59,660, or just under one-third, featured reinstatement orders.
The case is Vizguerra-Ramirez v. Blanche.

Supreme Court rejects challenge to policy allowing judges to pause deportation cases
WASHINGTON (TNND) — The Supreme Court on Tuesday cleared the way for the Trump administration to restrict a Biden-era policy allowing immigration judges to temporarily close thousands of deportation cases.
According to The Washington Post, the justices rejected an appeal by three cities and an immigrant rights group that sought to preserve the policy. It gives immigration judges discretion to remove certain cases from their active schedules without dismissing them.
The practice, known as administrative closure, allows judges to manage overwhelming caseloads while giving some migrants, including crime victims and neglected children, time to pursue legal options to remain in the United States.
Critics call the procedure a form of backdoor amnesty.
The practice has existed in various forms for decades. Approximately 360,000 migrants have received administrative closure since 1990, according to government statistics.
The Biden administration formally established the policy in 2024 after the first Trump administration attempted to prohibit its use.
When Trump returned to office in 2025, his administration stopped defending the rule. Texas challenged it in federal court, and a judge issued a permanent injunction blocking the policy.
Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut, along with an immigrant rights group, unsuccessfully sought to intervene before appealing to the Supreme Court.
The justices offered no explanation for rejecting the appeal.
Although administratively closed cases are not automatically reopened, they remain pending and could be returned to active deportation proceedings.

The request came from three cities—Baltimore; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio—and from nonprofit legal aid organization Centro Legal de la Raza.
The court’s denial was one sentence long without any explanation, a standard practice for emergency requests, and there were no reported dissents.

“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” the cities and organization wrote.
Administrative closure used to be common, with immigration judges using the tool to clear packed dockets, especially when a person had proceedings that could prevent their deportation such as a visa petition or appeal of a criminal conviction. Conservative politicians in places like Texas argue that the practice allows immigrants without legal status to stay in the country indefinitely.
The Biden administration tried to make the practice permanent in 2024, but after Trump returned to the White House, the Department of Justice announced it would no longer defend administrative closure. Tuesday’s ruling follows Friday’s federal appeals court decision that immigrants aren’t entitled to bond hearings. A whistleblower worried that Patel would use the chaos surrounding the files’ release to shed more federal employees.

FBI Director Kash Patel has been accused of threatening staff charged with redacting the government’s files on Jeffrey Epstein, and using their mistakes as an excuse to fire them.
In a complaint made in March 2025 and obtained and published Tuesday by The PunchUp, a whistleblower who worked for the FBI’s Information Management Division described the chaotic, high-pressure process of readacting the Epstein files for release.
“The director has threatened to fire [FBI staff] if the job is not done by his made up deadline, and has already tried to slim down the FBI,” the whistleblower wrote. “What better way than to fire us during this ever changing process, or as scapegoats for the DOJ’s lack of proper procedures.”
The complaint came as the Department of Justice shed thousands of employees.
John Sullivan, former section chief in the intelligence division, told The New York Times in January that Patel had berated employees on the redaction team during a conference call, telling them to work faster and that he’d fire anyone who didn’t meet his deadlines—a claim that is now reinforced by the whistleblower’s accusation.

“I am concerned that the rush deadline on the project, for no [discernible] reason, will lead to mistakes that could destroy people’s lives,” they wrote.
Catherine Sheehan Bruno, assistant FBI director and chief ethics and compliance officer, responded to the complaint on March 24, 2025, saying she was obliged to report the allegations. The following day, an FBI lawyer confirmed that the employee was willing to be identified to the inspector general. Then the FBI closed its own case. sources.text:
WASHINGTON (CN) — The Supreme Court denied an emergency appeal from Democratic-led cities on Tuesday, refusing to block a deal between Texas and the Trump administration ending a longstanding immigration practice through friendly litigation.
The cities say a Texas judge ignored their request to defend the Biden-era rule and instead rushed to approve an agreement between the state and the Department of Justice terminating the policy. They urged the Supreme Court to step in, warning against allowing the case to become an example for leveraging court rulings to achieve desired policy without the necessary review process.
Without explanation, the justices refused to do so. There were no noted dissents.
At issue is a 2024 rule codifying a longstanding practice allowing immigration judges to temporarily pause removal proceedings under certain conditions. The practice, known as administrative closure, could be used when an individual was pursuing protections through the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. And advocates say it often helped law enforcement secure cooperation from immigrant crime victims and witnesses.
Two years after the Executive Office for Immigration Review adopted the rule, Texas filed a lawsuit, claiming the policy exceeded the agency’s authority. The Lone Star State argued it allowed individuals without legal status to remain in the U.S. indefinitely.
Hours after the filing, Texas and the Department of Justice jointly asked the lower court to declare the 2024 rule unlawful and vacate it. They also requested the court prevent the Justice Department from enforcing the rule or enacting similar regulations in the future.
Later that day, Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor, a George W. Bush appointee in the Northern District of Texas, agreed to eliminate the 2024 rule nationwide and permanently restricted the federal government from adopting similar protections in the future.
Legal services provider Centro Legal de la Raza moved to intervene along with the cities of Baltimore, Maryland, Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut. The cities said if the judgment were to result in more deportations of noncitizens as Texas suggested, it would harm their revenue because their taxpayers would be deported.
Centro Legal de la Raza, which represents immigrants facing removal proceedings, said the judgment imposed substantial uncompensated legal work on the group.
Under what is known as rulemaking-by-collusive acquiescence, a new administration that is hostile to a regulation by its predecessor can leverage litigation brought by a friendly party to circumvent the Administrative Procedure Act’s requirements. The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza said this case represents an “egregious new extension of this phenomenon.”
But the Trump administration urged the Supreme Court to not put the “cart before the horse,” stressing the cities and Centro Legal de la Raza lacked standing to intervene. The government said any objections to the merits of the consent judgment were not a substitute for that prerequisite.

Let that sink in.
A prosecutor’s office, entrusted with seeking justice for victims, circulated advice on how to structure a plea so a defendant’s immigration problems might become a little less troublesome.
Where, exactly, does the child fit into this calculation?
A House Judiciary Committee report examines immigration-related practices in the offices of New York City’s district attorneys. Among the material cited is a 2019 Bronx guide on immigration-conscious plea bargaining. In cases involving children, it advised prosecutors to offer a plea deal on an offense that didn’t include the child’s age as an element of the crime, according to the article’s description of the report.
The distinction is important: The reported guidance concerns the elements of the offense used in a plea. It doesn’t establish that prosecutors were instructed to erase a child’s age from every document in a case. Nor does publicly available material identify a particular child sex case in which the instruction was used.
Even so, why should avoiding deportation be part of the exercise? Prosecutors have plenty to consider when evaluating a plea: the evidence, the victim, the appropriate punishment, and the chances of securing a conviction. Preserving a defendant’s ability to remain in the United States shouldn’t be a prize tucked into the negotiations.
The reported Bronx guidance didn’t stop there. Prosecutors were also encouraged to keep a domestic relationship out of the record of conviction in domestic violence cases, and to consider stalking charges without certain elements that could bring immigration consequences.
A woman allegedly beaten by her partner might reasonably expect prosecutors to focus on the violence. Instead, the guide reportedly gave them a reason to consider how the relationship appeared in the conviction record.
What a comforting set of priorities.
In Queens, District Attorney Melinda Katz’s own office describes what happened in other cases. During her first year in office, it says, she agreed to reduce or vacate the convictions of 21 defendants to avoid immigration consequences that weren’t anticipated when they pleaded guilty. Some were allowed to plead again to lesser offenses.
The office doesn’t identify the offenses or establish that all 21 defendants were in the country illegally. Those details matter, and New Yorkers deserve to know them. What the office does say is revealing enough: Its actions helped defendants avoid immigration consequences through valid guilty pleas.
Supporters can call deportation a harsh collateral consequence. Victims might call it a foreseeable result of committing a crime while subject to immigration enforcement. Either way, the public should know when prosecutors make avoiding it part of the deal.
Another question: What happens when immigration authorities release people who are then arrested again?
In a separate 2018 review, ICE said nearly 40 people were arrested again by local police after being released from New York City custody. One man was arrested on an assault charge, released, and later arrested on a robbery charge, ICE said.
Each of us, especially New Yorkers, deserves current, case-specific answers. How often were immigration-safe pleas offered? What were the original allegations? How many defendants were later arrested, and for what?
A prosecutor’s first responsibility is to seek justice. If officials adjust pleas to help defendants avoid immigration consequences, they owe victims and the public a full accounting.

Supreme Court declines to restore policy allowing immigration judges to close deportation cases
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to unfreeze a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration judges to use their discretion to temporarily close deportation cases for immigrants.
In an unsigned order, the court rejected a request from three cities with large migrant populations -- Baltimore as well as Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut -- to pause an agreement between Texas and the Trump administration that threw out the policy.
There were no noted dissents.
The regulation, known as "administrative closure," gives immigration judges discretion to temporarily pause deportation proceedings for migrants while the migrants seek humanitarian protections or other forms of legal status in the country.
The Trump administration has pushed to curtail judicial processes for unlawful migrants, and the high court's conservative majority has been largely deferential to executive authority in the area of immigration policy.
Deportation hearings in immigration court are legal proceedings initiated by the Department of Homeland Security in which an immigration judge determines whether a migrant should be removed from the United States. Often, an immigration judge will pause or dismiss a case to allow the individual to pursue legal relief.
While dismissals were viewed as a positive outcome for migrants, immigration attorneys have said the Trump administration, as part of its immigration crackdown, began to use dismissals to detain people at immigration courts and place them into expedited removal without allowing them to fight their case.
Last year, federal agents arrested hundreds of migrants at immigration courts -- in some cases after their deportation cases were dismissed.
In court filings, the cities argued that administrative closure promoted "efficiency" and protected "due process rights." They also argued that the practice has existed in various forms for decades.
In June, the state of Texas sued the federal government, arguing that the policy granted "indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country."

sources.news_title: Supreme Court blocks immigration judges from pausing deportation cases
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court declined to reinstate immigration judges’ longstanding authority to temporarily shelve deportation cases using “administrative closure.”
The decision keeps in place an agreement between the Trump administration and Texas that bars administrative closure while litigation continues.
The big picture: The emergency request was brought by three cities – including Baltimore – and an immigrant legal advocacy group, but the justices issued a brief order without public dissents or explanation.
- Administrative closure has been used for decades to manage immigration court dockets, especially when other pending proceedings could affect an individual’s removal.
- Critics, including Texas and the Trump administration, argue administrative closure allows undocumented immigrants to remain in the U.S. indefinitely, effectively granting amnesty.
Driving the news: The Biden administration in 2024 had finalized a regulation allowing administrative closure to continue, replacing a 2020 rule from Trump’s first term that was blocked by courts.
- After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department said it would not defend the Biden-era rule and worked with Texas to void it.
- U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor in Texas permanently blocked the Biden regulation nationwide after a joint request from the Trump administration and Texas.
Go deeper: Baltimore, New Haven, Columbus, and Centro Legal de la Raza tried to intervene to defend administrative closure, but were denied.
- The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals refused to pause O’Connor’s decision while an appeal is pending.
- The cities and advocacy group allege the federal government “colluded” with Texas in “manufactured litigation” to eliminate a disliked regulation.
- The Supreme Court’s move means immigration judges cannot currently use administrative closure to pause deportation cases.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to step into a legal fight over a Biden-era immigration policy that gave immigration judges authority to pause certain deportation cases.
The justices rejected an appeal from Democratic-led cities that argued the policy helped protect crime victims and neglected juveniles and should be restored.
Texas and the Trump administration agreed to a court order blocking the policy after Texas filed a lawsuit. The state contended that the use of administrative closure expanded sharply under former President Joe Biden, effectively allowing some immigrants to remain in the United States indefinitely.
Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut, joined the legal group Centro Legal de la Raza in seeking to defend the regulation. After a judge denied their request to intervene, the cities and group filed an emergency appeal with the Supreme Court.
Represented by Democracy Forward, they argued that Texas and the Trump administration had coordinated to secure a permanent court block on the regulation while avoiding the public rulemaking process.
The Justice Department urged the justices to reject the appeal, arguing that the cities lacked legal standing to challenge the settlement and had not demonstrated that they faced immediate legal harm.
